fullText: from above. It looks like a planet of its own. Forests roll beneath the airplane window for hour after hour without a single road. Rivers wider than cities pour north toward the Arctic, and the horizon never quite arrives. Somewhere far below, chimney smoke rises from a village perfectly straight into the freezing air. This is Siberia. It stretches from the Eural Mountains all the way to the Pacific, larger than the United States and all of Europe put together. And for most of the world, its name means exactly one thing. Cold. Here is the strange part. Millions of people call this land home. They chose it. They were born to it. and they love it in a way outsiders rarely understand. Head lies a city where the fish market works outdoors [music] at minus50. No freezer required. The catch standing upright in rows like bundles of firewood. And hidden among these snows, you will find a golden desert with real dunes and a great lake whose ice sings in the dark. [music] Today we cross this misunderstood land from east to west. From a school that only closes below - 52 to a train that takes 7 days to ride, chasing one question. What did the rest of the world get wrong about Siberia? Stay with us to the end of the line. You will meet a baby mammoth that slept for 50,000 years. A woman who lives two weeks walk from her nearest neighbor. And an answer far warmer than you expect. [music] In deep winter, the biggest city on permanent frozen ground disappears into its own [music] breath. 300,000 people live here. But at minus 50, the air cannot hold their warmth. It turns to fog, a dense white veil that swallows the streets whole. From the hills, only the chimney columns show, rising straight as fence posts. Somewhere inside that cloud, an entire city is calmly going [music] about its morning. And the best place to watch that calm is the outdoor fish market. There are no freezes here because of the whole city is one. White fish pulled from the rivers freeze [music] solid within minutes and are sold standing upright, packed in rows like firewood, hard enough to knock together with a sound like wooden bells. Sellers in fur stand beside their frozen bouquets for hours, cheeks glowing, trading gossip. [music] Nothing spoils. Nothing hurries. The city itself is engineered around the frozen ground beneath it. Every building stands on concrete legs lifted above the perafrost so its warmth cannot melt what everything rests on. Water pipes cannot be buried so they run above the streets in silver insulated sleeves looping over doorways like handrails. And from November to March, engines are simply never switched off. Parked cars hum through the night, a whole city idling like a herd of sleeping animals. We should be honest. This cold is not a postcard. Eyeglasses frost over in a minute and can crack. Phone batteries die inside a warm pocket. Bare skin must never touch metal. [music] And every year, some families decide one winter too many and move away. Taxi drivers here keep spare mittens on the seat for forgetful [music] passengers. Yet the schools open, the buses run, and mothers walk toddlers to kindergarten [music] wrapped like small round parcels, only their eyes showing. [music and bell] Watch those school gates for a moment and Siberia's first secret comes into focus. Nobody here is fighting the cold because a fight you cannot win is not worth having. They organize around it, dress for it, build for it, [music] and then get on with their lives inside it. And if you think this city is extreme, there is a village a day's drive east where all of this counts as mild weather. [music] The village of Oyakon [music] sits in a mountain valley that traps cold air like a bowl traps water. About 500 people live here and beside the road stands [music] a monument bearing a number -71.2° [music] C recorded a century ago. the lowest temperature ever measured in a permanently inhabited place. This is not a research [music] station. It is a village with grandmothers, wood smoke, and a school bell. [music] And that school [music] has the most extraordinary closure policy in the world. Classes are cancelled only when the thermometer falls below -52. For students older than 11, the bar is higher still, [music] -56, which means children here routinely walk to their lessons through air colder than the surface of Mars on a mild day, mitten hand [music] in mitten hand, and consider it a completely ordinary Tuesday. [music] The village animals match the village children. Yakutian [music] horses, shaggy and short-legged, live outdoors the entire year, growing coats [music] like bears and digging through snow with their hooves to reach [music] last summer's grass. They have been recorded standing calm in cold approaching minus [music] 70. No stable, no blanket. Fos born in autumn meet minus 60 before they ever see their first [music] spring. As one herders joke goes, the horses think winter is simply weather for horses. Out on the long road that connects these settlements, the cold has written its own law, and every driver obeys it. You do not travel alone. You do not switch the engine off [music] for long. And above all, you never ever drive past a car stopped on [music] the roadside. Because at these temperatures, a stranded driver has hours at most. Out here, stopping [music] to help is not kindness. It is a duty as fixed as the ice. That unwritten rule may be the most Siberian thing in this entire journey. The distances are enormous. The towns [music] are tiny. And so the people in between hold each other up like links in a chain. The cold wrote the rules. The people [music] keep them without ceremony every single day. And the same frozen ground that tests the living has been [music] quietly guarding the dead for 50,000 years. [music] [music] Everything Yakutsk [music] needs arrives on the water. The Lena River runs 4,400 [music] km through eastern Siberia. And for four short months of summer, [music] it becomes the city's supermarket, fuel line, and post office at once. Barges stacked with flour, timber, and machines glide between banks of pine. Watch the docks in August, and you understand the river is not scenery here. The river is the reason the city exists. [music] Then October [music] comes and the river changes jobs. The lena freezes meter thick and the authorities do something that sounds like fiction. They put up [music] road signs on the ice. Official winter highways open across the frozen surface with [music] speed limits and weight limits, and trucks drive up the middle of the river for months, delivering [music] supplies to villages no summer road has ever reached. Downstream, [music] the river shows off its oldest work. The Lena pillars rise straight [music] from the bank. A wall of stone towers begun half a billion years ago. Standing in ranks like a city built before anything could walk. But the true archive lies underfoot. Siberia's perafrost has stayed frozen through tens of thousands of winters, and everything that ever fell into it is still there, unchanged. A library [music] written in ice. And sometimes the library returns a [music] book. In the summer of 2024, near a vast Thor crater that local people call the doorway to the underworld, searchers [music] found a baby mammoth. She is the best preserved ever discovered anywhere on Earth. [music] Trunk, lips, and ears still intact. one year old when she [music] died at least 50,000 years ago, perhaps far older. Scientists [music] named her Jana after the river beside her resting place. [music] Jana now lies in a laboratory in Yakutsk, a few streets from the frozen fish market where visitors cue to see her the way other cities queue for famous paintings. She is a one-year-old from the ice age [music] delivered to the modern world by the same frozen ground that people here build their houses on. In Siberia, the past is not buried. It is merely waiting. [music] And at the far eastern edge of this land, we find the places where the present itself grows thin. Fly [music] east until the land runs out and you reach Chukotka, where the tundra meets two oceans. Its capital, Anadia, greets the endless white with open defiance. Every apartment block is painted, orange, crimson, sky blue, sunflower yellow. Whole walls turned into murals. In a place where winter [music] erases every color for 8 months, the people simply painted their own. From the air, the town looks like a handful of candy dropped on a white tablecloth. [music] Farther along the Arctic coast lies Peave, the northernmost town of this entire land mass. Once five times [music] more people lived here. Most have gone south. And the honest truth is that life this remote asks more than most are willing to give. Supplies come by plane and by ship. And yet a [music] few thousand remain. Dock workers, teachers, families, people for whom the silence and the pay and the strange bright summers add up to enough. Those who remain speak of the town [music] less like an address and more like a post they have chosen to hold. South of there on the wild coast of Sackelin Island stands the loneliest building in this whole journey. The Anva Lighthouse was raised in 1939 on a bare rock in the sea. a sevenstory concrete tower where keepers once lived for months with only the waves for company. Their lampguided ships threw some of the roughest water in the Pacific and storms burst against the base in slow explosions of spray. Later, machines replaced the keepers [music] and eventually even the machines fell silent. Today, the tower stands empty. Seabirds nest in the lamp room. Storms wash through the lower floors and photographs of it travel the world because there is something in that image nobody can look away from. A stone candle standing [music] alone in the sea, still upright long after its light has [music] gone out. painted towns, half empty harbors, a lighthouse with no keeper. This is the far edge of Siberia, where you can watch the tide of human settlement [music] advance and retreat like the sea itself. The map ends here, but the story does not because west of this coast live people who never needed the map at all. In the far northwest stretches the Yamal Peninsula, flat treeless tundra [music] running to the horizon in every direction. In the language of the people who live here, Yamal means the end of the world. They named it that themselves [music] and then they stayed for more than a thousand years. In winter, the temperature sinks below -50 and the wind owns everything that [music] stands taller than the grass. [music] The Nets are among the last true [music] nomads on Earth. Each year they move with their reindeer along a migration route of up to a thousand km. The whole family traveling by sled. Children, elders, puppies, holes, and all. At every stop, the women raise the chum, a cone of reindeer, hide over long wooden poles, and have a warm home standing on the bare tundra in under an hour. [music] The reindeer is not their livestock. It is their entire world walking. It is transport and food, coat and boots, tent walls and trade goods. Nothing is wasted. Even the antlers become tool handles and children's toys. Herders read their [music] animals the way sailors read water. A shift in the herd's mood can mean wolves [music] or weather or thin ice ahead. In return, the people go where the reindeer need to go season after season. exactly as their ancestors did. Children here grow up inside that rhythm. A Net's boy can drive a sled team across frozen ground before he can read a single word, and his sister can name every reindeer in a herd of hundreds. On winter nights, the aurora unrolls green across the whole sky, and the only sound in the world is breathing. Human, dog, and reindeer inside the [music] warm cone of the chum. Stand on Yamal in January and every instinct says no one could possibly live here. And yet in front of you, laundry drying stiff in the wind. Children laughing between the sleds, tea steaming inside the tent. That is the answer taking shape at the heart of this whole journey. What the world calls the end of the earth. These families simply call home. A thousand years of winters have not managed to argue them out of it. [music] At Siberia's far southeastern corner, the frozen story turns to fire. The Kamchatka Peninsula hangs [music] between two seas, unreachable by any road from the mainland, and it holds more than 300 volcanoes. 29 of them alive. Steam [music] rises from white cones above green valleys. Locals [music] fly between towns the way other regions ride a bus and every window seat is a geology lesson. The ground here does not sleep, it breathes. [music] In April [music] of 1941, a young geologist named Tatianaova was surveying a frozen [music] river canyon with her local guide, Anisphor Kupin. They stopped to rest on a [music] snowbank and the ground beside them suddenly exploded, throwing a column [music] of boiling water 10 m into the winter air. Anova had just discovered something science said this continent [music] did not have geysers. [music] She named that first geyser Pervenets, the firstborn. Until that day, the world knew of geysers in only three places, Iceland, New Zealand, and the American Yellowstone. [music] Costova spent years mapping the hidden canyon. She had found a valley where nearly 200 hot springs [music] steam between snowbanks. It is a place where you can stand with ice at your back and boiling earth at your feet a few steps apart. [music] Kamchatka's other giants walk on four legs. This peninsula holds, by most counts, the densest population of brown bears on [music] the planet. Every summer, when the salmon rivers fill, the bears line the banks like fishermen [music] at a pier, enormous, patient, utterly indifferent to the volcanoes, [music] smoking on the horizon behind them. Cubs learn the trade beside their mothers, slapping at fish half the size of their own bodies. [music] And the people of Kamchatka have made a quiet bargain with all this [music] fire. Geothermal plants turn volcanic steam into electricity [music] and heat for the towns below. Hot springs, warm green houses under the snow. It is the engine room of [music] the planet. and the locals live on top of it the way people elsewhere live beside a river with respect and without much fuss. On cold mornings, whole towns sit under a soft [music] white veil of their own volcanic steam. [music] Now for the first promise about the strange places. Deep in the tiger east of Lake Bal, the forest suddenly opens onto sand [music] dunes. The Charara sands are a true golden desert. 10 km of [music] wind sculpted ridges rising 30 m high, surrounded on every side by snowy peaks and pine forest. In winter, snow lies on the dunes [music] like frosting on bread. In summer, the dune tops bake warm enough to sting bare feet. Locals say it looks like a mirage. It is not. The Alai Highlands answer with a landscape from another planet entirely. In the Kaisel Chin Valley, the hills roll out in bands of red, orange, ochre, and violet. Minerals laid down over hundreds of millions of years, stripped bare for anyone to walk across. People call it the Mars of Siberia, and photographs from here regularly get mistaken for another world. A short drive away, a small lake stares upward like a pair of turquoise eyes. Underground springs push pale blue clay into rings on its floor, redrawing them gently all day long. [music] Then there is the lake that turns pink each summer. Blooms of microscopic algae and clouds of tiny brine shrimp fill the [music] salt water of Berlin Skoya, dying it rows and crimson from shore to shore. People have harvested salt here since the 1700s and an old railway runs straight [music] across the lake bed. So a few times a day, a train glides slowly through open pink water as if someone had laid tracks across a sunset. [music] The stone country keeps its own wonders. On a bare plateau in the northern eurals [music] stands seven rock towers, each over 40 m tall alone in the wilderness. Geologists explain them patiently. 200 million years of frost and wind. The Many people who have always lived here [music] tell it differently. Seven giants, they say, were crossing the mountains and were turned to [music] stone midstride, standing beneath them in the wind. The second version is easier to believe. And still, Siberia holds wonders back like savings it refuses to spend. The Piranana Plateau, far above the Arctic Circle, hides 25,000 lakes and more waterfalls than anyone has finished counting. And it can be reached only by helicopter. No roads, [music] no towns, no queue. Entire national parks worth of scenery waiting in silence for almost nobody. This land is not empty. It is simply bigger than our ability to visit it. Every journey across this land [music] eventually bends toward one blue giant. Lake Bal is the deepest lake on Earth, over 1,600 m down and the oldest at roughly 25 million years. It holds about a fifth of all the unfrozen fresh water on the planet. Stand on its shore and the far side [music] is often invisible. This is not a lake so much as a sea [music] that wandered in land and decided to stay. [music] And now the second promise. In deep winter, bal freezes into a lid of ice a meter and more thick, clear as window glass with [music] white methane bubbles hanging inside it like strings of pearls. [music] And on still nights the ice sings. As it tightens and cracks, deep notes roll across the darkness for kilometers. Booms, groans, sudden ringing tones. The voice of a frozen sea talking to itself under the stars. [music] The people of the lake treat that ice as a season of its own. In February, fishermen drive out in convoys across [music] the frozen surface, following routes that are checked and marked, drilling through a meter of ice to reach the [music] water below. Whole fishing camps appear out there each February, complete with tents and tea stoves. It is beautiful and it demands respect. The lake keeps its own rules and the locals follow them the way sailors follow tides. [music] ICOL even keeps its own animal mystery. The Nerper is the world's only freshwater seal, round as a barrel, found here and nowhere else on Earth. Science still argues about how a seal, a creature of the oceans, [music] ever arrived in a lake in the middle of a continent. And the Burriat elders smile and [music] say the lake keeps what belongs to it. The Nerper sunbathing on the ice in its thousands offers no comment. [music] [music] At the lakes's heart rises island, sacred ground for the Burat people. On its western [music] shore, the twin peaks of Cape Burken stand in the water beside poles hung with blue, white, and yellow prayer ribbons. Each [music] one a silent wish left to the wind. Legends even whisper that a great conqueror of the steps was born somewhere on this island. Visitors tend [music] to fall quiet here without being asked. Some places simply request it. In the south, where the land folds up against the mountains, runs the Chuya Highway, which many travelers rank among the loveliest drives [music] anywhere on Earth. It rolls for hundreds of kilometers past turquoise rivers, open step and stones carved by nomads thousands of years ago. Then at the Katuyaric Pass, the road simply drops [music] off the edge. Nine gravel switchbacks stitched down an 800 m canyon wall into a valley where herders still raise horses and yaks [music] below waterfalls. The valley ends at Lake Telkcoya, dark, cold, and so clean that [music] locals swear the water can be drunk straight from the surface, and that its taste [music] changes after a storm. The Alai people call it a sleeping spirit, and it is guarded by the highest mountain in all Siberia. Beluca, two white summits joined by a razor of ice. Old beliefs told quietly here for generations name Beluca the gateway [music] to Shambala, a hidden land of peace somewhere beyond the visible world. [music] These mountains also guard the most extraordinary household [music] in this entire story. Nearly as a century ago, a family quietly left the world behind and walked [music] into the deep tiger of the Sion Range. They built a cabin by a remote river, planted potatoes, and raised four children in a forest [music] where no path led to them. For decades, no one on Earth knew they existed. Then in 1978, geologists flying a survey over the mountains saw something [music] impossible below. A garden in the middle of 250 [music] km of wilderness. When they landed, they were met by a family who spoke an old careful form of [music] the language and who were astonished to learn how much the world outside had changed [music] while they were gone. The youngest daughter, Agaffia, was born in that forest [music] in 1944. She has never lived anywhere else. Today in her 80s, she remains on the family [music] homestead by the Abacan River with her goats and her chickens. The nearest neighbor 2 weeks [music] away on foot. Officials have offered many times to move her to a village. She always declines politely. The loneliest [music] woman on earth is not lonely at all. She is home. [music] There is [music] one thread that stitches all of these worlds together and it is made of steel. The railway across Siberia runs 9,289 [music] km, the longest in the world, crossing eight time zones between [music] the capital and the Pacific. It was built between 1891 and 1916. [music] And in its first decade alone, workers laid 7,000 km of track through forest and swamp. No railway on Earth has ever grown faster. [music] Riding it end to end takes 7 days and the train becomes a small traveling village. Strangers share tea from the samura at the end of each [music] carriage and the corridors smell of black tea all day long. Chess games stretch across whole afternoons. Someone's grandmother insists you take her extra pushki. By the third day, nobody remembers what they were in a hurry about. [music] The stations are the heartbeat of the journey. At small platforms deep in the tiger, the train pauses and local women appear at the windows [music] selling hot potatoes wrapped in cloth, smoked fish, and berries in paper cones. Passengers lean out into air that smells of pine and [music] coal smoke. Buy supper through a window and wave as the platform slides away. It is the oldest supermarket in Siberia and it never closes. And through the glass, the whole of this journey replays [music] in reverse. The step where horses graze, the blue flash of Bal, an hour of it filling every window on the southern side. The tiger [music] running beside the train for days like a green sea. Somewhere beyond the horizon, the frozen fish markets, the painted towns, the reindeer roads, the singing ice. Seven days, one window, and a land that never repeats itself once. [music] So, let the train answer the question we have carried from the start. The world looks at this land and and sees the hardest place on earth to live. The people who live here look back and see something else entirely. Not a trap of ice, but the only place wide enough to hold their kind of life. The world called it the end of the earth. They looked around, unpacked, and called it the beginning. And after 7 days of watching it roll past the window, you begin to suspect they were right all along. [music] If Siberia turned out warmer than you expected, a like helps this [music] journey reach the next curious traveler. And subscribing keeps a seat saved for you on the next one. Before you go, tell us one thing below. Could you ride all seven days of that train? And which window would you choose, the lake or the forest? We read every answer and they quietly steer where this [music] channel goes next.
